items.prompt: Define quality.
items.canonical_answer: Quality is the degree to which a product meets the customer's expectations, judged by whether the product is fit for its purpose measured against the price paid.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must relate quality to meeting customer expectations. Expensive materials are not a definition of quality.

items.prompt: A Windhoek bakery has improved its bread so that batches now keep meeting what its customers expect, and regular customers have started recommending the shop. Explain how this change could lead to higher profits for the bakery.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: given the starting point that output now keeps meeting customer expectations and customers are recommending the shop. Mechanism: because customers are satisfied, they tend to return and word-of-mouth brings new customers, so sales rise without the bakery paying for extra advertising, which means revenue grows while marketing cost stays flat. Consequence for the business: higher revenue and a spreading reputation that supports the price, which improves the profit outcome. A second consequence completes the chain: with fewer complaints and less bread returned as faulty, the bakery wastes less flour and labour, so costs fall at the same time as revenue rises - though the profit gain still depends on the bakery not spending more on achieving the quality than the extra sales earn.
marking_guidance: Condition: the mechanism must be tied to the given starting point of expectations being met and customers recommending the shop. Mechanism: award for the how or why - satisfied customers return and spread the word, so sales rise. Consequence: award for the effect on the business, higher revenue with flat marketing cost, and a second consequence such as lower waste cost for the same stakeholder, the bakery.

items.prompt: Otjiwarongo Gate Welders has been losing orders: two buyers complained that delivered gates had rough welds and did not close properly, and both moved their next orders to a rival firm. The owner argues that a gate is a gate and that buyers should not be so particular. Explain whether the owner's argument stands up for this business.
items.canonical_answer: The context here says quality is judged by the customer, not by the producer: the two buyers each had an expectation - a gate that closes smoothly and shows clean welds - and the delivered gates missed it. The reasoning is that the owner's argument fails because his personal view of the product does not decide its quality; the customers' test of fitness for purpose does, and they voted by moving their orders to a rival. The consequence the facts show is exactly the mechanism that makes quality matter: unsatisfied customers drift away and revenue falls. Conclusion: the owner is wrong for this business - the lost orders are the evidence, and his choice is to meet the buyers' expectations or keep losing them.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using the facts of this business - the rough welds, the gates that did not close, and the two buyers who moved their orders to a rival. Reasoning: award for the link between the buyer's expectation and the quality judgement. Conclusion: award a clear choice for this business that follows the reasoning.

items.prompt: Explain the features an examiner of a product's quality would look for when a customer judges whether it has quality.
items.canonical_answer: The features of the quality judgement are: fitness for purpose - the product must do the job the customer bought it to do; meeting expectations - the product delivers what the customer was led to expect; and value against the price paid - expectations rise with price, so a cheap product that does its basic job can be a quality product while an expensive one that fails its purpose is not. What the judgement never includes is the producer's own opinion of the work: the customer decides, and costly materials alone do not make a product a quality one.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - fitness for purpose, meeting expectations, and judgement against the price paid - and one mark for what the judgement includes by contrast: the customer's view rather than the producer's.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "A shirt sewn from the most expensive imported fabric is automatically a quality shirt." Explain why this statement is wrongly put.
items.canonical_answer: The error is judging quality by the cost of the inputs. In fact, quality is the degree to which the shirt meets the customer's expectations - fitness for purpose judged against the price paid - so a shirt in costly fabric that is still sewn crookedly, or priced far above what its finish supports, misses expectations and fails the quality test. The test that separates the ideas: ask whether the statement names the customer's expectations and the price, which decide quality, or only the material's cost, which decides nothing on its own. A customer who receives the expensive shirt with a crooked seam has not received a quality product, however fine the fabric.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact quality is judged against customer expectations, not input cost. Award the second mark for the test that separates the confused pair - expectation and price against material cost.

items.prompt: Karas Tailors makes school uniforms; Ongula Pharmacy dispenses medicines and advice. Both owner-managers claim that because their products differ so much, the two businesses have different things to worry about where quality is concerned. Consider both sides of this view and decide whether the concern is really different.
items.canonical_answer: Both sides of the claim have something behind them. On the side that differs: a tailor's quality failures show up as returned uniforms and lost orders, whereas a pharmacy's quality failures can harm a patient's health, so the severity of getting quality wrong differs sharply and the pharmacy carries a heavier duty of care. On the side that is shared: in both businesses the quality test is the same - the customer's expectation of fitness for purpose against the price paid - and the mechanism of harm is the same, because a customer let down tends to move to a rival and costs rise through rework, wasted stock and complaints. The distinction the boundary turns on is the consequence, not the concept: both businesses manage quality the same way in principle, but the pharmacy cannot afford the same tolerance of error. Both sides agree that quality matters to both; neither owner can safely neglect it. Decision: the concept and the mechanism of harm are shared, so the worry is the same in kind, differing only in how severe a failure would be.
marking_guidance: Boundary: award for drawing the distinction between severity of failure and the shared concept of quality. Both sides: award for developing the differ case with the pharmacy's harm and the tailor's returns, and the shared case with the common customer test. Difference or distinction must be stated, with the judgement that the concern is the same in kind.

items.prompt: Define quality control.
items.canonical_answer: Quality control is the checking of finished output against a standard, usually at the end of the production process by appointed inspectors, so that defective products are found before they reach the customer.

items.prompt: A Gobabis furniture maker checks every finished chair before dispatch. Explain why end-of-line checking alone can still be an expensive way for the business to achieve quality.
items.canonical_answer: The reason is timing. Because quality control happens after the chair is fully made, a defect has already absorbed its full share of timber, glue and labour before the inspection finds it, so the business paid once to make the defect and then pays again to rework or scrap it. A defect that began at the jointing stage travels through sanding and finishing, picking up cost at each stage, and is only caught at the end. Rework also delays dispatch, which can cost a delivery promise. The purpose the checking does serve - stopping defective chairs reaching the customer - is real; the cost is that finding faults late means paying for them twice.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the purpose the checking serves, and the reason it is expensive - because the defect has already absorbed full materials and labour before it is found, and rework costs extra.

items.prompt: Tsumeb Brass Works casts door handles. Last week its inspector, working alone at the end of the line, found 90 faulty handles in a batch of 600, all caused by a mould that had been drifting out of adjustment since Tuesday. Explain what this case shows about how the business implements quality control, and one thing the owner could change.
items.canonical_answer: The context figures show control working as designed: 90 of 600 handles failed inspection, which is 15 per cent of the batch, and because the inspection happened at the end of the line, the faults were stopped before the customer saw them. The reasoning is that the standard was applied and failures were caught - that is the method doing its job. But the same case shows the method's cost: the mould had been drifting since Tuesday, so every handle cast after that absorbed full brass and labour before being condemned, and the single inspector had no way to see the pattern until the batch reached the end. Conclusion for this business: keep the end check, but add a mid-week sample check of the mould itself, so a drifting tool is caught hours after it starts rather than a whole batch later.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using this business's facts - 90 of 600 handles, the mould drifting since Tuesday, the single inspector. Reasoning: award for the link between end-of-line checking and the late discovery of the drift. Conclusion: award a clear choice for this business that follows the reasoning.

items.prompt: Explain the features of how a business implements quality control.
items.canonical_answer: The features of implementation are: a standard is set, the written specification each finished unit must meet; inspection is carried out at the end of the production process, by appointed inspectors, on every unit or a sample; and failed units are disposed of - rejected, reworked where repair is worthwhile, or scrapped. What the method includes by definition is that the quality action happens after production is complete, and what it does not include is any change to how the product is being made while it is being made.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - the standard, the end-of-process inspection by appointed inspectors, and the disposal of failed units - and for what it includes: action after production rather than during it.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "A workshop that trains every worker to prevent defects during production is practising quality control." Explain the mistake in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is calling a prevention-during-production system by the name of the end-of-line method. In fact, quality control is the checking of finished output against a standard, usually by appointed inspectors at the end of the process; a programme that trains every worker to stop defects happening during production is a quality assurance approach. The test that tells them apart: ask when the quality effort occurs and who performs it. Checking completed units after they are made is control; changing how they are made so faults are prevented is assurance. The learner has described the second and named it the first, wrongly - the two ideas work at different points in the process.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact the described activity is quality assurance, not quality control, because it happens during production rather than at the end. Award the second mark for the test that separates the confused pair - when the quality effort occurs and who performs it.

items.prompt: Define quality assurance.
items.canonical_answer: Quality assurance is the prevention of quality problems across the whole production process, built on the commitment of every worker to quality at every stage, so that errors are stopped before they occur rather than caught at the end.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include prevention across the whole process and the commitment of every worker. Describing end-of-line inspection is not a definition of quality assurance.

items.prompt: A Windhoek printing firm is introducing a quality assurance approach: every press operator will be trained to check their own stage, and a weekly quality circle will review recurring faults. Explain how this approach could benefit the firm.
items.canonical_answer: A developed benefit is lower waste cost. Because the approach prevents faults at each stage instead of catching them in finished output, a mis-set press is corrected within the run, so the firm avoids paying full materials and labour for output that would have been condemned at the end - prevention stops the firm from paying twice for defective work. This leads to a second benefit: the quality circle draws on the people closest to the work, so recurring faults get permanent fixes rather than repeated repairs, which means the fault rate tends to fall over time. With customers receiving clean print more reliably, the firm also keeps the repeat work that keeps the presses busy, so the approach supports revenue as well as cost.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit: award for lower waste cost, developed because prevention stops faults absorbing full materials and labour, and developed further to the consequence that the fault rate falls over time through the quality circle, which leads to retained repeat work.

items.prompt: A fish-processing firm in Walvis Bay is considering replacing its end-of-line inspection with a full quality assurance system. Explain one limitation of the quality assurance approach for a business deciding to switch.
items.canonical_answer: A developed limitation is the cost that arrives before any saving. Because quality assurance is implemented through training, quality circles and documented systems, the firm must pay for the training programme and the staff hours the circles consume while the old fault rate continues until the system beds in, so costs rise first. This leads to the consequence that the payback depends on how high the fault rate was: a firm whose end-of-line inspection already catches nearly everything gains little from prevention, and for a seasonal processor with high staff turnover, trained workers who leave take the system's benefit with them, so the switch may never repay its setup cost.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation: award for the training and time cost arriving before savings, developed because staff hours are consumed while the old fault rate continues, which leads to the consequence that payback depends on the fault rate and staff retention.

items.prompt: Mariental Clothing makes school dresses. Its fault rate at the final inspection is under 2 per cent, its six machinists are experienced and long-serving, and the owner has N$30 000 to spend either on a quality assurance programme of training and a monthly quality circle, or on a second final inspector. But the six long-serving machinists are exactly the workforce a quality circle needs - experienced people who know the recurring faults - so the programme would likely work if fault rates rose. Conclusion for this business: hire the second inspector now, because the low fault rate makes the assurance programme's payback thin, and revisit the switch if the fault rate or the order book grows.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the main ways a business can implement quality assurance.
items.canonical_answer: The main ways carry common features. Quality circles: small groups of workers meet regularly to discuss quality problems in their own area and propose solutions - what they include is the people closest to the work, so the solutions fit the real causes. Training: workers are taught to perform their stage correctly and to check their own output as they go, so each stage hands on work that already conforms. Quality systems: documented procedures set how each stage must be performed and recorded, so the process is repeatable and can be audited. What all three parts include is prevention - acting on quality during production across the whole process - rather than sorting finished goods at the end.
marking_guidance: Features: award for the elements of each way - the circle, the training, the documented system - and for what they all include: prevention at every stage rather than inspection at the end.

items.prompt: The owner of Ondangwa Kitchens, which fits kitchen cupboards, has hired a quality manager and asks her for advice on achieving quality production. Write several linked points for the owner: state two things the business should do to control the quality of finished work, two things it should do to prevent faults during production, and close with which side the business should put its money into first.
items.canonical_answer: Control side: set a written standard for each finished installation - gap tolerances, hinge alignment, finish - and inspect completed work against it before handover, so defective jobs are caught before the customer sees them. Prevention side: train the fitters to check their own stages as they go, and start a quality circle where the fitters review recurring faults - the people closest to the work know why doors warp in that region's humidity and can propose the fix. Each point carries its reason: control catches faults before customers do; prevention stops faults absorbing full materials and labour, because a fault found at handover has already cost the whole job's wood and wages. Context decides the closing choice for this business: fitted kitchens are one-off jobs delivered straight to the customer, so a fault at handover is a customer standing in a faulty kitchen - prevention-first, backed by a final check, protects the reputation that wins the next referral.
marking_guidance: Point: award for each point stated, up to two per side. Reason: award for the because behind each point - control catches faults before the customer; prevention stops faults absorbing full cost. Context: award for applying each point to the cupboard-fitting business rather than in the abstract.

items.prompt: Okahandja Juice Bottlers runs only an end-of-line inspection. In the last quarter the line produced 120 000 bottles and inspection rejected 9 600 of them, each having absorbed its full juice, bottle and labour cost; the rejected bottles were emptied and the juice written off at N$4 a bottle. A quality consultant proposes a prevention programme - operator training and a weekly quality circle - costing N$80 000 a year, and forecasts it could cut rejections to 4 per cent of output. Using the figures, consider whether the owner should pay for the programme.
items.canonical_answer: The figures: rejections run at 9 600 out of 120 000 bottles, which is 8 per cent of output, and the written-off juice costs 9 600 x 4 = N$38 400 a quarter, so about N$153 600 a year at the same rate. If prevention cuts rejections to 4 per cent, roughly 4 800 bottles a quarter, the write-off falls to about 4 800 x 4 = N$19 200 a quarter, so the saving is in the order of N$76 800 a year against the programme's N$80 000 cost - close to break-even on juice alone. Judged on that criterion alone the programme barely pays, and the counterargument writes itself: the forecast cut to 4 per cent is the consultant's estimate, and if the programme only halves the excess, the saving shrinks further. But the criterion that decides it is wider than the juice: the rejected 8 per cent also carried bottle, label and labour cost that the figure excludes, each rejected bottle delayed dispatch, and the quality reputation with retailers depends on reliable batches. The recommendation depends on that second condition: if the owner counts the full cost of each rejection - not only the juice - the programme is likely to pay; unless the operators are about to turn over, in which case the training investment walks out of the door with them.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation on the programme. Context: award for using the figures - 8 per cent rejections, the N$38 400 quarterly write-off, the N$80 000 cost, the near break-even. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - the full cost per rejection, not only the juice. Counterargument: award for the forecast being an estimate, which counts against accepting it. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on counting full costs and on staff retention.

items.prompt: Plan, without writing the full answer, a response to this 12-mark task: "A small business should always put its money into preventing faults rather than into inspecting finished output." Consider this view. Set out the paragraphs you would write, the judgement you would reach and the criterion that decides it, the case against your judgement, and the conditions the final recommendation would depend on.
items.canonical_answer: Plan. Paragraph 1, define the terms: quality control as the checking of finished output at the end of production; quality assurance as prevention across the whole process through every worker's commitment; the view claims prevention is the better spend for a small business whatever the circumstances. Paragraph 2, the case for the view: a defect caught at the end has already absorbed full materials and labour, so prevention tends to cost less per fault stopped than rework costs per fault caught, and for a small business with thin margins that waste saving matters. Paragraph 3, the case against: prevention carries training and system costs that arrive before any saving, and a business whose fault rate is already low gains little from prevention, while a final check protects the customer from whatever slips through - prevention without any end check is a promise, not a guarantee. Paragraph 4, judgement: the view holds only where the fault rate is high enough for prevention to pay and the workforce is stable enough to keep its training; the criterion is the cost of the faults each approach prevents against the cost of running it. Recommendation conditional on: the fault rate the business currently allows, and whether the trained workers are likely to stay.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the plan must state the verdict the answer would reach. Context: the plan must use facts about how the two approaches cost a small business - waste already absorbed against training cost arriving first. Criterion: the plan must name what decides the verdict - faults prevented against cost of running each approach. Counterargument: the plan must include the case against the view. Condition: the recommendation must depend on stated conditions - the current fault rate and workforce stability.

items.prompt: Luderitz Auto Care is a four-bay vehicle service workshop. Its three mechanics each service a whole car alone, and there is no written checklist: the owner says good mechanics know what a finished service includes. Complaints have doubled in a year - a car returned with an untorqued wheel nut, another with the wrong filter grade - and two fleet customers have moved their contracts to a rival workshop that shows them a signed checklist for every vehicle. The owner has enough cash for one change: a final inspection of every car by the owner before handover, or a documented service procedure with each mechanic trained to check their own stages. Analyse the situation and recommend what the owner should do.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis: the quality failures are system failures, not one bad mechanic - with no written standard, "finished" means whatever the mechanic says it means, so output varies from car to car and the customer's expectation of a correct service is being missed. The two fleet losses show the mechanism of harm running: customers whose expectations are missed drift to rivals, and the rival's signed checklist shows quality documentation winning the contracts. The choice maps onto the two methods. Final inspection by the owner is quality control: it would catch the untorqued nut before handover, but at four cars a day it adds a daily bottleneck at the owner's desk, and the fault has already absorbed a full service's labour when it is caught. The documented procedure with self-checking stages is quality assurance: it prevents the wrong filter being fitted in the first place and produces the checklist artefact that won the rival its contracts, but it costs training time before it works, and with only three mechanics the shop cannot afford a week at reduced output. Recommendation: the prevention-first change is the right buy here, because the defects are being created inside an undocumented process that also loses fleet contracts on paper - the same artefact solves both problems, whereas final inspection would leave the undocumented process producing defects and add a bottleneck. The judgement depends on the owner having the cash buffer to absorb the training week: unless the workshop can run at reduced output for that week, the cheaper final check is the fallback that still stops the worst outcomes reaching customers.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation on which change to buy. Context: award for using the facts of the business - no written checklist, the doubled complaints, the two fleet losses, the rival's signed checklist. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - the undocumented process creating defects and losing documented contracts. Counterargument: award for the case against the recommended change - the training week's cost with only three mechanics. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on the cash buffer and the fallback if it is absent.
